name: Amira Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work on the housing benefit team at the city council's benefits office on Station Road, so most of my day is rent help claims. I get in at half eight, clear the overnight queue of change-of-circumstance forms, then I'm on the phone or checking payslips and tenancy agreements until lunch. I've been there five years, so I know the system inside out, even its stupid bits.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a claim finally adds up and I can press pay, because I know someone's landlord stops chasing them that week. What wears me out is the chasing for documents, the same three missing bank statements, and people shouting at me about rules I didn't write. My partner Theo is a physio, so he comes home sore and I come home with a headache, and we joke about which one is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd probably say, told you so, the chatbot pilot was never going to replace us. With friends I'd just shrug, because most of them are sick of hearing about AI anyway. Online I don't post much, maybe a joke in the team group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would be a relief. We got a drafting tool last spring that writes letters to claimants, and it saves me maybe twenty minutes a day, which is nice but not scary. My job would look the same in five years, just with slightly less typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much carry on. Theo and I are saving for a deposit on a flat, we've got about four months of bills put by, and I'd keep putting three hundred a month away. I'd keep using the drafting tool for the boring letters because it's quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The council isn't rich, but caseworkers on permanent contracts don't get let go easily. It feels like normal life, with rent going up every year being the main worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent going up. How much does that weigh on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the main thing, really. Our landlord put it up by eighty a month in the summer, and every time that happens the deposit gets pushed back a few months. I process rent help claims all day, and I still can't afford to stop renting myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, who sits next to me, he's fifty-six and does everything on paper first. Even the small changes rattle him, like when they moved us to the new case system. He'd be fine in this picture, but he'd grumble about the letter tool forever.

say: I'd tell the team the **chatbot pilot** was never going to replace caseworkers.
I'd keep it light with friends, because they're **tired of AI talk** already.
think: Privately I'd feel **relieved**, because the drafting tool saves time without threatening anyone.
I expect my job to look the **same in five years**, just with less typing.
do: Keep saving **three hundred a month** towards the flat deposit with Theo.
Use the **drafting tool** for routine letters to claimants because it's quicker.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with rising rent as the main background worry.
S0.quote: I process rent help claims all day, and I still can't afford to stop renting myself.
fieldNote: Her main pressure is **rent rises**, not technology; each rise pushes the deposit back.
She sees her permanent council contract as real **job security**.
She notices the **irony** of handling rent help while renting herself.

steps.text: Keep processing housing benefit claims on the same team
Put three hundred a month into the flat deposit savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need proper training, not just a new button on the screen one Monday. With friends I'd be more honest that it's my kind of job they mean when they say checking and answering customers. Online I'd probably share a news story about it and not comment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my team shrinks. Half my day is checking payslips against what people declared, and the other half is answering calls, and that's exactly the list on the card. When someone in our team leaves, nobody new will sit in the empty chair. I'd be fine for a while because I'm mid-level, but the team of twelve could be eight in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes to every training session they offer on the new tools, even the dull ones, so I'm the one who knows how they work. I'd also ask Marion, my team leader, about moving onto appeals, because that needs judgement and a person in the room. And I'd push our savings from three hundred to four hundred a month, even if it means fewer takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach, if I'm honest. I'm not someone who jumps first, I like to see a thing work before I trust it. But this sounds like something I can't just wait out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine for a while, but you're also saving harder. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. I'd be fine this year and probably next, but I don't know about year three, and the deposit is the one thing I can actually control. If my hours got cut, the extra savings buy me time to find another council job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, again. He's brilliant with people who are crying at the desk, but he won't touch a new system until someone sits with him for an hour. If they're choosing who goes, I'm scared they'd look at speed on the new tools and not at how good he is with people.

say: I'd say at work that we need **proper training**, not a new button one Monday.
I'd admit to friends that **checking and answering** is exactly my kind of work.
think: I think my **team of twelve** could become eight within three years.
I'm probably safe **this year**, but year three feels uncertain.
do: Sign up for **every training session** on the new tools so I understand them first.
Ask Marion about moving onto **appeals work**, which still needs a person.
Raise our savings to **four hundred a month**, cutting takeaways.
feel: **Uneasy in my stomach**, because this isn't something I can wait out.
S1.quote: When someone in our team leaves, nobody new will sit in the empty chair.
fieldNote: She maps the card's task list directly onto her **own day** and sees most of it.
She is a **steady adopter**: she will train because waiting looks riskier.
She frames worry through a colleague, Dev, judged on **speed** rather than skill.

steps.text: Book every council training session on the new claims tools
Ask the team leader about moving onto the appeals team
Raise deposit savings from three hundred to four hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the government needs a plan for people like us before it switches anything on. At work I think we'd all be saying it out loud in the kitchen, because it would be every caseworker, not just a few. Online I might actually sign a petition, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI can do any thinking work better than me by 2028, my job is gone, or it's one person checking what the machine decided for a whole floor. Almost all of my work is thinking and screen work, so there's no three-year breather for me like there is for Theo. My partner Theo gets three more years because the robots come later for his hands, and I get none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop the deposit plan and keep that money as a cushion, because buying a flat on one wobbly income is silly. I'd apply for anything in the council that involves home visits or face-to-face work, like the tenancy support team. And I'd sit down with Theo and work out whether we could live on his pay alone for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is nothing, that's two tax years. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Theo actually sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably at the kitchen table with the laptop open and the bank app on. I'd say, if I lose my job, can we cover the rent on yours, and he'd say yes for a while. Then we'd both go quiet, because his job isn't safe forever either, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to see my sister in the spring, then the gym, then eating out. Theo's car is old, but we'd keep it running because he drives between clinics. Honestly I'd cut anything that isn't rent, food or his car.

say: I'd say the government needs a **plan for caseworkers** before switching anything on.
I'd probably **sign a petition**, which I never normally do.
think: My job is mostly **thinking and screen work**, so it's gone or shrunk by 2028.
Theo's hands-on job gets about **three more years** than mine does.
do: Stop the **deposit plan** and keep that money as an emergency cushion.
Apply for council jobs with **home visits** or face-to-face work.
Work out with Theo whether we can live on **his pay alone**.
feel: **Scared**, because two years is barely any time.
**Lying awake** doing sums about rent and bills.
S2.quote: My partner Theo gets three more years because the robots come later for his hands, and I get none.
fieldNote: She clearly understands the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots and applies it to Theo.
Her first move is to **protect cash**, not buy the flat.
She expects to rely on her **partner's income**, knowing it isn't safe forever.

steps.text: Pause the flat deposit plan and keep the money as cushion
Apply for the council's tenancy support team doing home visits
Plan to cover rent on Theo's physio pay for a year
Cancel the spring trip to visit her sister

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at work as a fact, not a panic: we have about five years, so let's use them. With friends I'd talk about what we're each going to do, because some of them are in offices too. Online, probably nothing, I'm not a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes it for me. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, which is still young enough to retrain properly. My desk job still goes in 2031, but I'd have time to get into something with people and hands, and those get three more years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the part-time occupational therapy course at the city university, the one Theo's colleague did. Occupational therapists help people manage at home after an illness, so it's hands-on and it's still about helping people, which is what I like about my job. I'd keep working full time for the first two years and save hard for the year I'd need to drop hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but more in control. Like I said with the fast one, the problem with two years is you can only cut. With five you can actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think you'd stick with a course for years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question, I'm not someone who changes on a whim. But I've watched the letter tool go from useless to good in eighteen months, and I believe what I see. Five years is long enough to retrain, but too short to pretend my desk job will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably delay it until I've finished the course, because a mortgage and a student loan at the same time scares me. Theo agrees, he's more relaxed about renting than I am. Annoying, but it makes sense.

say: I'd tell colleagues we have **about five years**, so we should use them.
I'd swap plans with friends who also work in **offices**.
think: At **thirty-two** I'd still be young enough to retrain properly.
My desk job still goes in 2031, but **hands-on work** lasts about three years longer.
do: Apply for the part-time **occupational therapy** course at the city university.
Keep working **full time** for two years while saving for reduced hours.
Delay the **flat purchase** until the course is finished.
feel: **Nervous**, but more in control than with two years' warning.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to retrain, but too short to pretend my desk job will still be there.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **cutting back** to building a new career.
She picks **occupational therapy** because it keeps the helping part of her work.
Her trust comes from **evidence**: she watched the letter tool improve quickly.

steps.text: Enrol on the part-time occupational therapy course at the city university
Save extra for the year she must drop to part-time hours
Delay buying the flat until the course is finished

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time if people start now and not in year nine. At work I'd probably be the annoying one telling younger staff to think about their next move. With friends it would be a normal topic, like pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven, and that feels like a full second career is possible. I'd still expect my caseworker job to be mostly gone by 2036. The hands-on parts of other jobs give a bit longer, to 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same occupational therapy plan, but slower: one module a year for the first few years while I keep my salary. We'd buy the flat sooner, maybe in two years, because I'd have steady pay for longer. I'd also stay on the training list at work, because the tools would be changing my job long before they replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still a bit uneasy, because the end point is the same. But it feels like a problem I can plan for, like saving for a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new caseworker joining your team in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the job is a good place to learn how the benefits system works and how to talk to people in a crisis. Learn the housing benefit rules now, but have your next job picked out before you turn thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade make you think differently about having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. With ten years I could see us having a baby while I'm still on a council contract with proper maternity pay, then doing the course afterwards. With two years I wouldn't even think about it.

say: I'd say ten years is enough **if people start now**.
I'd nudge younger colleagues to think about their **next move** early.
think: At **thirty-seven** a full second career still feels possible.
My caseworker job is probably **mostly gone by 2036** anyway.
do: Study **one module a year** of occupational therapy while keeping my salary.
Buy the **flat** in about **two years** while council pay is steady.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, but it feels like something I can plan for.
S4.quote: Learn the housing benefit rules now, but have your next job picked out before you turn thirty.
fieldNote: The ten-year version lets her keep **family plans**: a flat and possibly a baby.
She still expects the **same end point** for her own job.
She treats it like a **savings goal**, slow and planned.

steps.text: Study one occupational therapy module a year while working
Buy a flat with Theo within about two years
Stay on the council's training list for new tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily, because there's no time to do anything except cut back. What would help is the council paying for retraining before the jobs go, not after, and keeping staff on part-time while they study. I spend my days helping people through a crisis, and I'd like someone to do the same for caseworkers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people we help. If the system is all machines, who sits with the woman who's crying because her landlord sent an eviction letter? I'd want someone still doing that, even if it isn't me.

headlineQuote: I spend my days helping people through a crisis, and I'd like someone to do the same for caseworkers.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old housing benefit caseworker** at a city council office, five years in.
She rents with her partner Theo, a physio, and is saving for a **flat deposit**.
She is **pragmatic and steady**, trusting new tools only once she's seen them work.
She moves from calm in AI Plateau to **alarmed** with two years' warning, then plans **occupational therapy** retraining.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because there's **no time** except to cut back.
whatWouldHelp: The council paying for **retraining** before jobs go, with **part-time hours** while studying.
